opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think people tend to underestimate the technical side and overestimate how clear the business case is, but the truth is both are hard, and they're tangled together in an interesting way.

On the technical side, building a nose on a chip is genuinely difficult. With vision you had the CCD and then CMOS sensors, which gave you a clean, reproducible, digital representation of light. With hearing you have the microphone. Smell has never had its equivalent. Biology solves the problem with hundreds of different receptor types, each binding a wide range of molecules in combinatorial, overlapping ways, and they're constantly regenerating. Replicating that breadth, sensitivity, and stability in hardware that doesn't drift, doesn't get poisoned by humidity or by whatever it smelled last, and can be manufactured at scale is a very deep engineering challenge. People have been building electronic noses for decades, and most of them work in a narrow, carefully controlled setting and then fall apart in the real world.

But the business-model uncertainty might be the bigger risk, because it shapes what you even try to build. If you say "I'm building a general-purpose nose," the natural question is: who pays for that, and for what? A camera was useful because there was an obvious thing to do with images. With smell, the applications are scattered: food quality and spoilage, fragrance and flavor development, agriculture, environmental monitoring, safety, potentially medical diagnostics. Each one has different requirements for sensitivity, cost, form factor, and regulation. A sensor that's great for detecting a gas leak is nearly useless for telling you whether a fragrance smells like fresh-cut grass.

So my view is that you can't resolve those two uncertainties separately. You have to pick problems where the technical bar is reachable and someone has real pain they'll pay to solve, then use that to fund and inform the harder, more general work. That's partly why I find the computational side so exciting. If you can build a good map of odor, a way to predict what a molecule smells like from its structure, that's valuable on its own today, for designing new molecules, for example, and it becomes the software layer a future sensor plugs into. You don't have to wait for the perfect chip to start creating value; you build the representation first and let the hardware catch up.

The trap is building a beautiful sensor in search of a problem, or chasing a business case the physics can't support yet. The balance is staying honest about both and letting each constrain the other.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's the question we had to answer before we ever wrote a line of code or spun up a wafer. Because when you look at why olfaction has lagged so far behind vision and hearing in terms of digitization, I don't actually think it's primarily a technical story. People have been building electronic noses since the eighties. The sensors existed in some form. What didn't exist was a clear answer to "who pays for this, and what do they do with the number that comes out?"

So the way I think about it is that there are really two curves. There's the technical difficulty curve, which is real. Smell is a massive space. There are something like forty billion possible molecules in the smell-able range, and you have to detect them at parts-per-billion or parts-per-trillion concentrations, in mixtures, in a world full of humidity and temperature swings and background noise. That's hard. But it's the kind of hard that engineers know how to attack. You can measure progress. You can run a benchmark. You can tell when you're getting better.

The business-model uncertainty is a different kind of hard, because it's not something you can brute-force in the lab. Nobody wakes up in the morning saying "I wish my phone could smell." There's no obvious consumer pull the way there was for cameras. So you have to find places where the ability to read chemistry in the air actually changes a decision somebody's making today. That's things like, is this food about to spoil, is this person's breath telling you something about their metabolic state, is there a leak in this facility, does this product match the reference lot.

And what we found at Osmo is that these two things are deeply coupled. You can't resolve the business question in the abstract, because the right answer depends on what the technology can actually do at a given cost and form factor. And you can't resolve the technical question in the abstract either, because "a nose on a chip" is underspecified until you know what you're sniffing for and how good you need to be. A chip that detects spoilage in a warehouse has completely different requirements than one that's trying to recreate a perfume.

So the way we've tried to balance it is honestly to refuse to balance it. We treat them as the same problem. We pick a wedge where we're pretty confident someone will care about the output, we build toward that, we learn where the technology breaks, and that reshapes which wedge makes sense next. And underneath all of that we're building the thing that doesn't change, which is the map. If you have a good predictive model of how molecular structure relates to perceived smell, that's an asset regardless of which application wins, and it makes every sensor you build dramatically more useful because you're no longer just reading a signal, you're reading meaning.

I'd say if I had to put weights on it, early on it was ninety percent business uncertainty and ten percent technical. Now that we've shown the map works and we've got a few real customers, it's shifting. The technical problems are starting to be the ones that keep me up at night, and frankly that's the place I'd rather be.

astra-6.text:
I think the technical difficulty is the dominant uncertainty right now. There are a lot of things you could do with a nose on a chip if it worked well enough—quality control in manufacturing, detecting something going wrong with food, potentially applications in health. But those applications have very different requirements, so saying there’s a market for an artificial nose doesn’t mean you’ve figured out a business.

The hard part is getting from a sensor that responds to some molecules in a controlled setting to something that reliably interprets smells in the real world. You’ve got mixtures, changes in humidity and temperature, and sensors that can drift over time. And then you need to turn that signal into information somebody can act on.

So I wouldn’t treat the business model as solved. But I’d put more weight on the technical risk. The useful thing is to find a narrow application where you can work backward from a customer’s decision: What do they need to detect, how reliably, and at what cost? That gives you a much more concrete target than trying to build a general-purpose nose all at once.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are two different kinds of risk, and you want to be careful about taking on both at once. With a nose on a chip, there’s still a fundamental technical question: can you build a sensor that captures enough information about the molecules in the air to tell you what something smells like, reliably and repeatedly?

Then there’s the business question: even if you could do that, who needs it badly enough to pay for it? There are lots of imaginable applications, but an application isn’t necessarily a business.

My instinct is to find a very concrete customer problem where the value is clear, and then take the technical risk required to solve it. You don’t have to solve all of olfaction on day one. You need to solve something useful, learn from that, and build toward the broader vision.
